candidateRows: A publicly demonstrable claim must produce independently confirmable physical manifestations through detectable interactions with shared reality.
This establishes the public-demonstrability test against which the later claims about consciousness, idealism, and supernatural interaction are examined.
Matt sets aside hard solipsism, assumes a shared universe, and explains how sensory exploration, independent confirmation, detectability, and repeatability ground warranted acceptance.
Idealism is an inference to the best explanation supported by mental correlations, top-down causation, and the failure to reduce consciousness to matter.
This supplies the principal affirmative evidential case that consciousness is fundamental rather than reducible to material processes.
Matt's requirement that extraordinary claims be supported by publicly demonstrable and independently confirmable evidence.
Michael invokes the evidential reasoning used for historical evolution, then cites correlations, quantum cognition, top-down causation, and philosophical arguments as converging support.
Evolutionary inference differs from the idealist inference because its component evidence is itself demonstrable, mutually reinforcing, and statistically accountable.
This challenges the affirmative analogy by arguing that a sound inference must be assembled from sturdy, independently demonstrable evidential components.
Michael's comparison between his idealist inference and the evidence-based inference supporting biological evolution.
Matt describes overlapping dating methods, anomaly handling, and statistical analysis to explain why evolutionary models remain reliable despite being inferential.
Occam's razor favors an idealist ontology because objects can be described through experienced properties and informational structure without positing an extra material substance.
This is a direct ontological argument for treating mental phenomena or information as sufficient and material substance as explanatorily unnecessary.
Matt's claim that experienced properties arise through interactions involving distinct physical objects, fluids, and their properties.
Michael argues that descriptions reduce to felt or perceived properties, compares reality to generated game content, and invokes bundle theory to deny a further substrate.
Physical properties and forces concern interactions that occur independently of mental experience, so removing physical components removes causal capacities rather than merely sensations.
This directly applies the physical-interaction test by grounding observable effects in mind-independent causal relations among physical systems.
Michael's claim that experienced properties and informational descriptions make a distinct material substrate unnecessary.
Matt argues that friction and nuclear forces do not require experience, using molecular behavior and water cutting metal to illustrate independent physical interaction.
Physics reduces to mathematics and information, and under idealism the relevant informational distinctions are phenomenal states rather than material arrangements.
This reframes the opponent's physical examples within an informational ontology and identifies the information at issue with discernible mental phenomena.
Matt's appeal to friction, nuclear forces, molecular behavior, and other interactions occurring without conscious experience.
Michael claims physics is mathematical and informational, invokes Shannon's framework, and says idealist information consists of distinguishable qualia, sensations, thoughts, and mathematics.
If all physical development depends on a mind, preconscious evolution and chemical interaction become unavailable unless a divine mind is added to sustain or collapse reality.
This exposes the central explanatory burden of theistic idealism by connecting observer dependence to cosmic history before ordinary conscious observers existed.
Michael's view that material appearances depend on mind while underlying reality is fundamentally informational or phenomenal.
Matt seeks clarification and argues that mind-dependent reality appears to preclude evolution and chemical interaction, thereby motivating the postulation of a divine observer.
A divine observer need not continuously watch events because the wave function evolves deterministically as information until conscious observation produces definite physical appearance.
This is the affirmative mechanism intended to reconcile an observer-linked physical world with evolutionary development occurring before local conscious observers.
Matt's objection that mind-dependent physical reality would prevent evolution and chemistry unless a divine mind continuously sustains collapse.
Michael denies a literal watching deity, maintains that information develops deterministically in the wave function, and assigns observers the narrower role of producing physical collapse.
The video-game analogy does not establish that unobserved structures cease to exist because a game engine can continue rendering or maintaining them off-screen.
This tests the affirmative explanatory analogy and argues that absence from an observer's display does not imply absence from the underlying reality.
Michael's video-game analogy for deterministic informational evolution followed by physical appearance when a conscious observer arrives.
Matt distinguishes the player, avatar, screen, and engine, noting that simulated rooms may remain maintained even when no player is viewing them.
Without thinking minds, interactions persist only as deterministic informational evolution and need not occupy definite positions in a spacetime setting.
This states the affirmative position on the debate's decisive counterfactual and specifies what remains when no conscious observer produces physical collapse.
Matt's insistence that friction, chemical processes, and molecular interaction must still occur if every thinking mind is removed.
Michael concedes interaction at the informational level but denies a need for definite spatiotemporal placement, appealing again to deterministic wave-function evolution.
The claim that physical reality would stop without thinking minds is unfalsifiable and violates Occam's razor.
This challenges the consciousness-dependent account on the core standards of public testability and explanatory parsimony identified by the motion.
Michael Jones's claim that everything would effectively stop without thinking minds to collapse the wave function.
After Jones confirms that a mindless universe would effectively stop, Dillahunty characterizes that position as resistant to falsification and needlessly complex.
The consciousness-dependent account is falsifiable because discovering hidden variables compatible with quantum mechanics would undermine it.
The move directly defends the pro position against the debate's public-demonstrability challenge by proposing an empirical route to falsification.
Matt Dillahunty's objection that the consciousness-dependent account is unfalsifiable and violates Occam's razor.
Jones answers the falsifiability criticism by invoking hidden variables, the Kochen-Specker theorem, contextuality, and measurement-dependent perceived reality.
